heading: Beavers, bison and berries
intro: Ecosystems change over time, and watching the same land, water and animals year after year is one way to see those changes. These connections show First Nations, Métis and Inuit knowledge and monitoring in Edmonton, across Alberta and across Canada. Each one links to the beavers, bison, berries and populations you study in this lab.

connections.title: amiskwacîwâskahikan: Beaver Hills House
connections.text: Even after the Hudson's Bay Company named the fort here, the people who came to trade kept calling it other names. The Cree called it amiskwacîwâskahikan (Beaver Hills House). The Nakota Sioux called it ti oda (Many Houses), and the Niitsitapi called it Amakowsis, or omahkoyis (Big Lodge). The Cree place name Amiskwaciy translates directly to Beaver Hills. Beavers still shape the many wetlands of the Beaver Hills. Like the pond in this lab, their dams create habitat for moose, waterfowl and other species, and support water quality and resilience to floods and droughts.

sources.title: City of Edmonton Archives: Before it was Edmonton
Nature Conservancy of Canada: Let's keep the beavers

connections.title: Askîy Guardians track berry health
connections.text: Askîy is the community-based environmental monitoring initiative of the Otipemisiwak Métis Government. Métis Citizens who report their observations of plants, fish and wildlife are called Askîy Guardians. In the berry health program, Citizens share what they find on berry picking trips, whether the harvest was good or poor, for berries such as saskatoon, blueberry, chokecherry and cranberry. As the program explains, berries are part of Métis stories, medicine and connection to the land. In 2024, 56% of Citizens who reported had enough berries for their needs, down from 64% in 2023. Reports gathered year after year can show changes in abundance, timing and health.

peoples: Niitsitapi (Blackfoot): Siksika, Kainai, Piikani and Blackfeet Nations
connections.title: Bison as ecological engineers
connections.text: Leaders of the Blackfeet, Kainai, Piikani and Siksika Nations launched the Iinnii Initiative to reconnect all Blackfoot Confederacy Nations with their buffalo culture and create a home for the buffalo to return to. Kainai Elder Dr. Leroy Little Bear says, "Bison are ecological engineers." Through grazing, wallowing and migration, bison fertilized soil, opened grasslands, held forests in check and created habitat for hundreds of other species. The Buffalo Treaty of 2014, whose signers include the Blackfeet Nation, Blood Tribe, Siksika Nation and Piikani Nation, recognizes buffalo as "a practitioner of conservation" and an important part of the ecological system.

sources.title: Yellowstone to Yukon Conservation Initiative: Bison are ecological engineers
Parks Canada (Fort Battleford): The Buffalo: A Treaty of Cooperation, Renewal, and Restoration

connections.title: Hunters counting caribou in Nunavut
connections.text: In Nunavut, hunters take part in a community-based monitoring program run by the Nunavut Wildlife Management Board. After a hunt, Richard Kakk of Kugaaruk records how many caribou he saw in the herd, how many were males and how many were females, and whether the herd looked healthy. Lars Qaqqaq, a hunter and trapper from Baker Lake, has noticed species moving north: "20 or 30 years ago we didn't have all these wolverines, or grizzly bears." Someone near Baker Lake even caught a beaver hundreds of kilometres from the nearest trees. The Nunavut Agreement requires management decisions to use both scientific knowledge and Inuit Qaujimajatuqangit (IQ).

sources.title: Mongabay: With the help of an app, Nunavut hunters document the changing Arctic (2020)

try: Beavers and bison both change the land around them. Using the beaver pond model, explain how one species can change abiotic factors and species diversity across a whole area. What might happen to stability if that species disappeared?

Richard Kakk records herd size, males and females, and herd health. Which level is he describing: species, population or community? Which of his observations could tell you whether the herd is stable, and what would you add?
Askîy berry reports went from 64% of Citizens having enough berries in 2023 to 56% in 2024. Is two years of data enough to say the berry population is changing? What else would you want to know?

slide.title: Beavers, bison and berries
points: Edmonton: the Cree called the fort here amiskwacîwâskahikan, Beaver Hills House. Beavers still build wetlands in the Beaver Hills.
Alberta: Métis Askîy Guardians track berry health, and Blackfoot Nations are bringing back bison, which Kainai Elder Leroy Little Bear calls ecological engineers.
Canada: Nunavut hunters count caribou and notice species moving north. Decisions there must use both science and Inuit Qaujimajatuqangit.
slide.notes: Use with Learn section 1 (beaver pond: ecosystems are dynamic) and section 4 (stability), or with the Elk Island levels in section 2. Ask: how can one species, like a beaver or a bison, change the biodiversity of a whole area? How do repeated observations over many years help us tell normal ups and downs from real change? Point students to the Ways of knowing section in the lab for sources and discussion prompts.

review_flags: Existing callout (Learn section 1) and the matching deck note: "Many First Nations and Métis families have watched the same lands for generations, noticing changes in berry crops, water levels and animal numbers." I found no source for that exact sentence. Conor Kerr's paper supports berries and animals but says nothing about water levels. Proposed sourced rewording, to apply to both the lab callout and the deck note if you approve: "Knowledge built over generations of harvesting is one way to see ecosystems change. Métis harvester Conor Kerr writes about Métis harvesting in the lands and waterways surrounding Edmonton, in Treaty 6 territory. He describes years when berries came in a full two weeks earlier than they should have, and moose showing up where they were not expected and missing from places where they have always been. He treats this experience as evidence, and as data." Source: Conor Kerr, "What the land knows: Métis harvesting narratives as climate knowledge", Canadian Climate Institute, https://climateinstitute.ca/publications/what-the-land-knows-metis-harvesting-narratives-as-climate-knowledge/ . Approve, edit, or keep the original.

Edmonton: the City of Edmonton Archives says the Cree called the fort amiskwacîwâskahikan (Beaver Hills House). I kept that to the fort and did not say it is the name of the whole city. The Nature Conservancy of Canada spells the area name Amiskwaciy (capital A, no circumflex). OK to show both spellings as each source gives them? I labelled the people nêhiyaw (Cree) in the peoples list, while both sources say only "Cree". Keep or change?

Edmonton: I tried to fetch Parks Canada's Elk Island beaver page to connect the Beaver Hills name to the Elk Island examples in the lab, but the fetch was blocked, so I did not claim that Elk Island is in the Beaver Hills. Want me to try again and add that link?

Bison: the main source is the Yellowstone to Yukon Conservation Initiative, a conservation group, not a Blackfoot organization, although it quotes Kainai Elder Dr. Leroy Little Bear. Would you prefer I look for a Blackfoot-run source (for example Blackfoot Crossing or a nation's own site) before this goes live? I did not state where each nation is located because neither fetched page says so plainly. The Buffalo Treaty text uses "Blood Tribe", the Y2Y article uses "Kainai Nation"; I used each as its source does.

Bison and the lab: the lab's Elk Island bison examples could link here, but I found that Elk Island has transferred bison to Métis Crossing and Beaver Lake Cree Nation only in an APTN article that mixes several years, so I left it out. Worth adding with a cleaner Parks Canada source?

Inuit: the Mongabay article (October 2020) is a journalism source, not Inuit-led. It does not state that Richard Kakk or Lars Qaqqaq are Inuit, and it does not say whether the program still runs. I labelled the connection Inuit because the article frames the program around Inuit Qaujimajatuqangit and the Nunavut Agreement. Do you want me to look for an Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami or Nunavut Wildlife Management Board source to replace or support it?
Askîy berry numbers (56% in 2024, down from 64% in 2023) come from the Otipemisiwak Métis Government page and may be updated each year. OK to quote percentages, or keep it qualitative?

Two connections are at the Alberta scale (Métis and Niitsitapi) because both fit the lab closely. I did not find a well-sourced fit tied to a specific Treaty 7 or Treaty 8 nation's own monitoring, or to the Métis Settlements, in the time available. Drop one Alberta connection if you want strictly one per scale.

Local partner: the deck already notes that a local community partner should be considered. If a Knowledge Keeper is willing to share, their own published words could replace or add to the Edmonton connection in a later revision.

Overlap across labs: the Banff bison project and the Buffalo Treaty also appear in the drafts for Energy Flow and Cycles and Disturbance and Succession. Keep it in both labs as a thread students can follow, or should I replace this one with a different connection (for example a Treaty 6 or Treaty 8 nation's own wildlife or wetland monitoring)?
